facts.title: Named for a Finnish chemist
facts.text: Gadolinium is one of the very few elements named after a real person: Johan Gadolin, a Finnish chemist who pioneered the study of rare earths in the late 1700s. The name traces back through the mineral gadolinite to Gadolin's work, and the element itself was isolated spectroscopically by Swiss chemist Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac in 1880. French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran prepared a purer sample in 1886.

facts.title: It rescues blurry MRI scans
facts.text: Gadolinium is the workhorse of magnetic resonance imaging contrast agents, with millions of doses given to patients every year. Its Gd3+ ion has seven unpaired electrons, giving it an enormous magnetic moment that speeds up how nearby water protons relax, brightening tumors and blood vessels on the scan. Because the free ion is toxic, it is always wrapped inside a tightly binding chelating molecule before injection.

facts.title: Seven unpaired electrons
facts.text: The Gd3+ ion has exactly seven electrons in its 4f shell, meaning each of the seven f-orbitals holds one electron, all spins aligned. This half-filled configuration is unusually stable and gives gadolinium one of the highest magnetic moments of any element. That same property is what makes it so useful in both MRI and magnetic materials.

facts.title: It gets cold when demagnetized
facts.text: Gadolinium famously shows the magnetocaloric effect: it warms up when placed in a magnetic field and cools when the field is removed. This makes it a leading candidate for magnetic refrigeration, a solid-state cooling technology that could one day replace gas-compression fridges and use far less energy. Prototype magnetic refrigerators built around gadolinium alloys have already been demonstrated.

facts.title: Magnetic near room temperature
facts.text: Most familiar magnets like iron stay magnetic well above everyday temperatures, but gadolinium loses its ferromagnetism at a Curie point of about 20 degrees Celsius. That means a chunk of pure gadolinium is strongly magnetic in your refrigerator but turns non-magnetic in a warm room. It is the only element besides iron, cobalt, nickel and dysprosium that is ferromagnetic at or near room temperature.

facts.title: A champion neutron absorber
facts.text: Naturally occurring gadolinium has the highest thermal-neutron capture cross section of any stable element, driven mainly by the isotopes Gd-157 and Gd-155. This makes it valuable in nuclear reactor control rods and as a burnable poison mixed into fuel to tame the reaction over time. The same hunger for neutrons lets physicists use gadolinium-loaded water to detect elusive neutrinos.

facts.title: Born in dying stars
facts.text: Like the other lanthanides, gadolinium is forged in the cosmos by the slow and rapid neutron-capture processes inside aging stars and during violent events such as neutron-star mergers. It does not occur as a free metal on Earth but is locked into minerals like monazite and bastnasite. Despite its rare-earth label, gadolinium is more abundant in Earth's crust than elements such as iodine or silver.

facts.title: No job in your body
facts.text: Gadolinium has no known biological role in any living organism and is not part of normal human chemistry. The free Gd3+ ion is actually harmful partly because it is almost the same size as calcium, so it can sneak into calcium channels and protein binding sites and jam them. This is exactly why medical agents keep it locked inside a chelate cage.

facts.title: Glows in your TV and X-rays
facts.text: Gadolinium compounds are excellent host materials for phosphors that glow when struck by radiation. Gadolinium oxysulfide is used in scintillator screens that turn X-rays into visible light for medical and security imaging, while gadolinium-based phosphors have appeared in color television and display technology. Doping these hosts with other rare earths tunes the exact color of light they emit.

facts.title: A metal that fights itself
facts.text: Pure gadolinium is a silvery, fairly soft and malleable metal, but it is reactive enough to slowly tarnish in moist air, forming a loose oxide film that flakes off and exposes fresh metal to corrode further. In dry air it is much more stable. Small amounts added to iron, chromium and related alloys improve their resistance to high temperatures and oxidation, a useful trick in demanding engineering applications.
